### The Tactical Utility Flight Test

**The flight programme flew 87 sorties in the tactical utility phase, of which 80 were scored. Those produced 407 engagements, of which 325 were scored.**
Six pilots from the International Test Organization flew in each condition. Reducing those to rates,

$$\frac{80}{87} = 92.0 \ \text{percent of sorties scored} \qquad \frac{325}{407} = 79.9 \ \text{percent of engagements scored}$$

$$\frac{407}{80} = 5.09 \ \text{engagements per scored sortie} \qquad \frac{325}{80} = 4.06 \ \text{scored engagements per scored sortie}$$

**Four scored engagements per sortie is a high rate and it is the direct product of the real-time kill determination described above.**
It is also the reason the flight programme reached a few hundred engagements rather than a few dozen.

The flight programme could not reproduce the simulation exactly, and the most consequential difference is an
envelope restriction.
**The aircraft was limited to a post-stall entry speed of 225 knots calibrated maximum, against 325 knots in the simulation**,
and the programme's own analysis put the effect of that restriction alone at a thirty percent reduction in
post-stall use, according to the [NASA history][ref_joyce_pdf]. Only the slow-speed line-abreast condition was substantially unaffected.

A later series raised the entry speed.
**The flight-test conclusion was that 265 knots calibrated was slightly better than 225 and that 300 knots would be desirable for a future fighter**,
which is a statement that the demonstrator was constrained below the useful value of its own capability.
The [NASA history][ref_joyce_pdf] lists that finding among the flight-test conclusions.

### What the Flight Testing Concluded

The conclusions of the tactical utility flight test, as the [NASA history][ref_joyce_pdf] sets them out,
are worth quoting in structure because they are more careful than the summaries built on them.

- Post-stall close-in combat at seventy degrees of angle of attack had overwhelming success.
- Flying the aircraft conventionally, limited to thirty degrees, showed that the benefits of
  post-stall technology were **greater than expected**.
- Operational guest pilots with minimal training could fight effectively using post-stall
  technology.
- The aircraft was very successful against the then front-line Navy fighters, the [F-14D][ref_f14] and the
  [F/A-18C][ref_f18].
- **Against opponents with superior thrust-to-weight ratios it was far less successful.** The
  Air Force [F-15C][ref_f15] and [F-16C][ref_f16] would not enter the close-in arena and escaped to an altitude
  sanctuary.
- Limiting the aircraft to 45 degrees of angle of attack was insufficient and 70 should be used.
- Advanced short-range missiles with greater angle of attack and off-boresight launch capability
  are highly desirable for an aircraft with post-stall technology.

**The fifth of those is the most important sentence the programme produced and it is almost never quoted.**
A manoeuvre advantage that applies inside a particular arena is worth nothing against an opponent who
declines to enter that arena. The F-15C and F-16C pilots of the 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron exploited
their thrust-to-weight advantage to stay above the fight.

**That is not a limitation of post-stall technology as implemented. It is a statement about what kind of advantage it is.**
An exchange ratio is not a property of an aeroplane. It is a property of an engagement, and the adversary
gets a vote on which engagement occurs.

### What the Pilots Said

**The pilots' own summary is more restrained than the fact sheet built on it, and the divergence between the two is documented.**

The flight-test paper delivered in July 1994 records that all the pilots on the programme had strong
military backgrounds and that one point they agreed on is that the aircraft
**does not necessarily represent a total revolution in air combat**. They would not advocate trading away
other important fighter characteristics to acquire the capability. What they concluded was that enhanced
pitch pointing and velocity-vector manoeuvring opened new options in close-in combat, as a repositioning
tool to drive the fight or as a way to rotate and point for a weapons employment the opponent cannot
counter, and that it must be used selectively and in a timely manner to succeed.

**The NASA fact sheet on the aircraft opens the corresponding passage by stating that the X-31 constituted a revolution in air combat in the post-stall region, and then reproduces the pilots' qualifications immediately afterwards.**
The two statements sit in consecutive sentences and the first inverts the source of the second. This is not
presented as an accusation of bad faith. It is an ordinary and very common thing that happens when a careful
conclusion is summarised, and it is recorded here because the summary is far more widely read than the
paper.

There is a second observation from the same paper that has aged well.
**Carefree handling removed the pilot's cues about energy state.** A conventional fighter warns its pilot
through buffet and degrading handling that the energy is going. An aircraft that remains docile throughout
its envelope gives no such warning, and the report names restoring those cues as a challenge for future
designs.

The wider literature on this subject is gathered in the clusters on handling qualities of highly augmented aircraft and on agility as a measured quantity in The Contemporary Literature. The records closest to this section are these.

- [Harper and Cooper 1984][research_harperjr_cooper_1984]
- [Hodgkinson et al 1988][research_hodgkinson_skow_1988]
- [Mazza 1992][research_mazza_1992]
- [Wilson et al 1993][research_wilson_riley_1993]
- [Hess 1994][research_hessronalda_1994]

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

**The X-31 is unusually well placed for this comparison because it ran the same experiment twice, once in a simulator and once in the air, and then ran the simulator experiment twice as well.**

### The Simulation Campaigns

Two manned simulation campaigns, called Pinball I and Pinball II, preceded the flight testing. The design
was systematic. Four pilots flew each week, one flying the adversary and the other three flying the X-31
with post-stall technology, which gives four groups of three pairings and therefore
**twelve pilot combinations per week**. Twelve combinations across four starting conditions gives
**48 engagements for each of six cases**, and 240 engagements were flown with the baseline configuration
against 192 with a modified high-lift configuration.

### Where the Two Simulations Disagreed With Each Other

**The two campaigns disagreed sharply, and that disagreement is data about the method rather than about the aeroplane.**

| Starting condition | Pinball I | Pinball II |
|---|---|---|
| Defensive | 1.2 | 0.47 |
| Offensive | 22 | 23 |
| Slow-speed line abreast | 20 | 6.67 |
| High-speed line abreast | 1.5 | 2.8 |

Taking the ratio of one campaign to the other condition by condition puts a number on the disagreement,
which is the comparison the measures-of-effectiveness literature would call a repeatability check,

$$\rho_i = \frac{E_i^{\text{I}}}{E_i^{\text{II}}}$$

| Condition | Pinball I | Pinball II | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Defensive | 1.2 | 0.47 | 2.553 |
| Offensive | 22 | 23 | 0.957 |
| Slow-speed line abreast | 20 | 6.67 | 2.999 |
| High-speed line abreast | 1.5 | 2.8 | 0.536 |

**The offensive condition reproduced to within 4.3 percent and the slow-speed line-abreast condition differed by a factor of 2.999.**
Writing $\bar{E}$ for the mean of a campaign's four conditions, the comparisons are

$$1 - \frac{22}{23} = 0.043 \qquad \frac{20}{6.67} = 2.999 \qquad \frac{2.8}{1.5} = 1.867 \qquad \frac{\bar{E}^{\text{I}}}{\bar{E}^{\text{II}}} = \frac{(1.2 + 22 + 20 + 1.5)/4}{(0.47 + 23 + 6.67 + 2.8)/4} = \frac{11.175}{8.235} = 1.357$$

The defensive condition differed by a factor of 2.553 in one direction and the high-speed line-abreast by
1.867 in the other. The means of the two campaigns are 11.175 and 8.235, a ratio of 1.357, so
**the campaigns agree far better in aggregate than they do anywhere in particular**, which is the signature
of sampling variation rather than of a systematic difference.

The programme's explanation for the defensive disagreement is that the use of post-stall technology on the
initial move differed. In Pinball I a standard initial move was used that usually neutralised the attacker's
advantage and turned a defensive start into an offensive situation. In Pinball II that move was used only
occasionally.

**That explanation is almost certainly correct and it is devastating for the measure.** It says that the
exchange ratio in the defensive condition is a measurement of pilot technique rather than of aircraft
capability, and that a change in the tactics the pilots chose moved the reported number by a factor of two
and a half with the same aeroplane and the same simulator.

**Set that beside the interval arithmetic above.** At twelve scored outcomes the defensive condition cannot
separate 0.36 from parity anyway. The two campaigns disagreeing by a factor of two and a half is therefore
not evidence that one of them is wrong. It is what a quantity with that much sampling variation looks like
when measured twice.

### The Simulation Also Disagreed With the Flight Data in a Way That Mattered

**The single most important disagreement is that the simulation did not predict the departure.** The
flight-test report states it plainly. The fidelity of the simulation was described as quite good and it
always lagged behind the flight data, and the report says the failure to predict the departure ahead of time
is the most dramatic illustration of that lag.

The mechanism of the lag is worth naming. The aerodynamic model was built from wind tunnel data and
corrected by parameter identification from flight, so
**the simulation could only know about an aerodynamic effect after the aircraft had flown into it**. For a
phenomenon like forebody vortex asymmetry, which is sensitive to a half-inch of nose radius and to Reynolds
number, that is a structural limitation rather than a modelling shortfall.

### The Wind Tunnel Did Not Give the Complete Picture

The flight-test report's first technical lesson is exactly that sentence, and it is specific about where the
tunnel fell short. Above fifty degrees of angle of attack the aircraft encountered lateral kicks the pilots
called lurches, which had not appeared on the small-scale model. The asymmetry data showed no
distinguishable trend against flight condition across a Reynolds number range of 1.5 to 4.0 million based on
a forebody diameter of about 3.2 feet, as the [asymmetry report][research_cobleigh_1994] gives it, which is
a narrow range and one reason the tunnel could not have settled the question.

**The comparison of flight against wind tunnel and water tunnel yawing-moment asymmetries became a research subject in its own right**,
with reports published in 1994 and revisited in 2001 and again in 2003.

### High Lift, and a Negative Result Worth Keeping

**A modification that should have helped did not, and the programme cancelled it on the evidence.** Flight
researchers recognised that a high-lift configuration would give the aircraft dramatically more lift below
thirty degrees of angle of attack. Without post-stall technology the high-lift aircraft outperformed the
baseline against the F/A-18, as expected.

**With post-stall technology the high-lift aircraft was slightly less effective**, because pilots gave up
post-stall opportunities trying to fly in the high-lift mode. The pattern was that a pilot able to exploit
high lift would fly post-stall until the fight went low and then drop below thirty degrees to use high lift
and avoid the hard deck, which turned the fight conventional. Since the aircraft's advantage was in
post-stall flight, the international test community decided against implementing high lift.

**A capability that improves the aircraft in isolation and degrades it in combination is a real finding**,
and it is the kind of result that only a manned simulation with free tactics can produce.

## What the Data Changed

### The Capability Was Adopted and the Aircraft Was Not

**Thrust vectoring entered production, and it did so on aircraft that did not need the X-31 to prove it was possible.**
The [F-22][ref_f22] carries two-dimensional vectoring nozzles. The F-16 multi-axis thrust vectoring
programme demonstrated three-dimensional vectoring on a production airframe during the X-31's own flight
programme, and the X-31 flight-test report cites it as evidence that incorporation is achievable without
significant trade-offs.

**What the X-31 contributed was not the mechanism but the evidence about employment**, and the evidence is
more qualified than the reputation. Post-stall manoeuvring supplements conventional performance and does not
replace it. It wins where the fight is slow and close and loses where the opponent can decline that fight.

### The Quasi-Tailless Result Outlived Everything Else

**The quasi-tailless demonstration is the part of this programme with the longest reach, and it was almost an afterthought.**
It established that an aircraft with no vertical tail at all could be held at supersonic speed by thrust
vectoring, at a divergence rate of 290 milliseconds to double.

Every low-observable combat aircraft since has faced the same problem, because a vertical tail is the single
worst feature an airframe can carry for radar cross-section from the side.
**The question of how to control yaw without a fin is now the central configuration question of unmanned combat aircraft design**,
and the answers in current use are split effectors, differential drag devices and vectoring. The X-31's
contribution was to establish that the vectoring answer works at a measured level of instability rather than
an assumed one.

There is a second and less-noticed result in the same experiment.
**Differential canard deflection was studied as a yaw generator with and without the vertical tail**, which
is a redundant-effector question of exactly the kind that modern control allocation exists to solve.

The wider literature on this subject is gathered in the cluster on unmanned combat aircraft and the tailless problem in The Contemporary Literature. The records closest to this section are these.

- [Simon et al 1993][research_simon_blake_1993]
- [Ngo et al 1996][research_ngo_reigelsperger_1996]
- [Bowlus et al 1997][research_bowlus_multhopp_1997]
- [Gillard et al 1997][research_gillard_dorsett_1997]
- [Paul et al 1997][research_paul_garrard_1997]

### The Accident Changed the Air Data System, Eventually

**The aircraft that was destroyed by a probe returned with no probe.** The second aircraft flew again from
2001 to 2003 in the Vectoring Extremely Short Takeoff and Landing Control Operation Research programme,
which used thrust vectoring to fly approaches at high angle of attack, and that aircraft carried a
**flush air data system** with no protruding probe to ice.

That is a satisfying arc and it should not be overstated. Flush air data systems were under development for
other reasons, principally for hypersonic vehicles where a probe cannot survive, and the X-31's second life
was a separate programme with its own objectives.
**But the pairing is real, and the flush system removes the exact failure mode that destroyed the first aircraft**,
because there is no single pneumatic path whose blockage can be shared by every computer downstream.

The Mishap Board's own recommendations were institutional rather than technical for the most part. It
recommended that the system safety analyses be redone with a focus on single-point failures, that a
mitigation for the loss of raw pitot-static data be found and verified in simulation, that temporary
operating procedures be reviewed and controlled, that all cockpit switches and displays be audited for
correct function and labelling, that programme personnel be trained in the basics of system safety, and that
the parachute be replaced with one of slower descent rate.

**The last of those is not a control-system finding and it belongs in the record.** The pilot descended
under a seventeen-foot canopy at approximately 28.3 feet per second, a rate typical for naval aircraft that
operate mostly over water, and was injured on the hard playa surface, as the
[NASA history][ref_joyce_pdf] records.

The wider literature on this subject is gathered in the cluster on air data, icing and flush air data sensing in The Contemporary Literature. The records closest to this section are these.

- [Larson et al 1987][research_larsonterryj_whitmorestephena_1987]
- [Whitmore et al 1992][research_whitmore_moes_1992]
- [Whitmore et al 1992][research_whitmorestephena_moestimothyr_1992]
- [Moes et al 1993][research_moestimothyr_whitmorestephena_1993]
- [Whitmore et al 1995][research_whitmorestephena_davisroyj_1995]
- [McLaren et al 2007][research_mclaren_jayashankar_2007]

### What Some Test Team Members Thought the Report Missed

**Not everyone accepted the Mishap Report's emphasis**, and the disagreement is instructive. Team members
felt that large airspeed errors and suspected icing should have mandated stopping the test until the
discrepancy was understood, and that the report placed too little weight on the test team's own methodology.
One is quoted saying that the test pilot and flight control engineers ought to understand the importance of
the right gains, and another that seventy-knot errors and icing conditions are not acceptable for good
flight tests.

**The lesson the programme's own pilots drew was procedural rather than technical.** Rogers Smith put it to
the Society of Experimental Test Pilots in 1996 as an instruction to speak up, stop the tests and think when
something does not make sense, and Ken Szalai, the Dryden director at the time, put it as calling a halt for
anything that does not sound, feel or smell right.

**Both formulations are about a failure of attention rather than a failure of engineering**, and the
arithmetic in this article supports that reading. The information needed to detect the failure was
displayed, spoken aloud, and independently available on a second instrument.

**The X-31 flew before three of the fields that now own its questions existed.** This section surveys the
modern literature on each, written from current knowledge rather than from the editorial date of the
article.

### Air combat effectiveness, simulation and measurement

**The keystone's own literature.** Measures of effectiveness, combat models, piloted and constructive air combat simulation, and the evaluation of fighters in engagements.

**The measure the programme reported has a literature of its own, and very little of it names the measure.** Measures of effectiveness and combat effectiveness appear in 38 of the 288 titles, and the [measures of effectiveness for general-purpose forces][research_pugh_mayberry_1973] that the exchange ratio belongs to are part of it. Beyond-visual-range combat appears in 21 titles, while the exchange ratio, the kill ratio and the loss exchange together appear in five, so the quantity the keystone section analyses is almost never the subject of a title.

### Air combat decision making by learned policies

**Air combat flown by software.** Manoeuvre decision making, situation assessment and engagement tactics produced by reinforcement learning, neural networks and other learned agents.

**The question the X-31 answered with six test pilots and a scoring radar is now answered with learned policies.** Of these 125 records, 77 name reinforcement learning or one of its algorithms, and 101 were published from 2022 onward. Beyond-visual-range engagements are named in 25 titles and within-visual-range, close-range or one-to-one engagements in 19. An agent trained against one adversary policy and one distribution of starting conditions learns an advantage conditional on both, and the aggregate win rate it reports is the same weighted mean this article has spent its keystone section unpacking.

**The modern work has one advantage the X-31 did not.** It can fly ten thousand engagements rather than four hundred, which moves the high-speed line-abreast case from unresolvable to routine.

### Rates, proportions and their intervals

**The arithmetic behind the keystone's second question.** Interval estimation and hypothesis tests for a binomial proportion, for two proportions and for rates, together with the choice of sample size.

**Much of this literature was written for medicine.** Of the 349 records, 199 name a binomial or a proportion, and 90 appeared in medical, epidemiological or biometric venues, which is one of the places where the inference on small counts that an engagement campaign needs has been worked out most carefully.

### Uncertainty quantification

**Intervals on computed quantities.** Uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analysis in aerodynamic, structural, propulsion and simulation models.

**A result with an interval attached is a modern expectation and it was not a 1993 one.** The X-31 published
point estimates of exchange ratios with no uncertainty statement, and the arithmetic in this article's
keystone section is an attempt to supply retrospectively what the discipline now supplies as a matter of
course.

### Pursuit, evasion and differential games

**The formal theory of the engagement.** Differential games, pursuit and evasion, capture and the value of a game, for aircraft, missiles, spacecraft and generic agents.

**The mathematical treatment of one-versus-one air combat as a differential game predates the X-31 by decades**, with [Isaacs on differential games][book_isaacs] as its founding text, and the programme's reports do not appear to draw on it. Of the 166 records, 54 predate 1990, the year the X-31 first flew, and they are the part of the literature the programme could have read. That literature poses the engagement as a two-sided optimisation with a value function, and the value at a given starting state is precisely the quantity the exchange ratio estimates by sampling.

**A formal treatment would have said in advance that the value depends on the starting state**, which is the article's central finding arrived at by arithmetic on published outcomes. The two literatures were solving the same problem in different buildings.

### Agility as a measured quantity

**The vocabulary of the pointing advantage.** Agility metrics, their evaluation by optimal trajectory analysis, and the manoeuvres that test them.

**The vocabulary of agility metrics was being invented while the X-31 flew**, and the modern literature has largely settled on the distinctions the period was reaching for, separating pointing agility from axial and torsional agility. The X-31's contribution to that vocabulary was to make the pointing component large enough to measure cleanly.

**The subject is concentrated in the decade of the programme.** Of the 76 records, 37 were published from 1985 to 1996 and 19 from 2015 onward.

### Post-stall manoeuvring

**Flight past the stall.** Supermanoeuvrability, post-stall manoeuvre control, post-stall aerodynamics and its models, and flow control at post-stall angles.

**The post-stall literature after the programme turned to control laws and to models of the regime.** The post-stall pitching manoeuvre and the Herbst manoeuvre are now control-design problems, and post-stall aerodynamic models are built for upset-recovery training and for simulation. **The manoeuvre has not moved to small aircraft in this literature.** Of the 103 titles, one names a small or unmanned aircraft, a micro air vehicle or a perching manoeuvre.

### High angle of attack aerodynamics

**The flow the aircraft flew in.** Vortex flows, vortex breakdown, wing rock, strakes and the aerodynamics of whole configurations at high angle of attack, measured and computed.

**The flow the X-31 could not predict is now computed**, and 60 of the 552 titles name a computation or a simulation. Analyses of the flow around the X-31 itself at high angle of attack have been published as validation cases more than a decade after the aircraft stopped flying, and they are listed under the vehicle's own literature below. **That is a fitting use of the data.** An aircraft that flew because the tunnel could not settle a question has become the benchmark against which the calculation that replaced the tunnel is judged.

The reservations are real. Forebody vortex asymmetry is sensitive to a nose radius of half an inch, to boundary-layer transition state and to Reynolds number, and those are the three things computation finds hardest.

### Yaw asymmetry and forebody flow

**The cliff in the departure analysis.** Asymmetric forebody vortices, their sources, and their control by strakes, blowing and nose shape.

**This is a literature of the programme's own period.** Of the 91 records, 56 were published from 1985 to 1996, when forebody vortex control was being tried on the F/A-18 and the F-15 as well as on the X-31.

### Thrust vectoring

**The means.** Mechanical thrust vectoring by vanes, paddles and vectoring nozzles, its integration with the airframe and its effect on manoeuvre.

**The X-31's mechanism is a small part of the vectoring literature.** Vanes or paddles are named in 7 of the 209 titles, and the rest concern vectoring nozzles, their integration and their effect on manoeuvre.

### Fluidic thrust vectoring

**Vectoring without moving parts.** Shock vector control, dual-throat and bypass nozzles, counterflow and Coanda vectoring.

**The X-31 chose paddles over a vectoring nozzle for weight and cost, and the modern answer removes the moving parts entirely.**
Fluidic vectoring deflects the exhaust by injecting a secondary flow into it, either by displacing the shock
structure in a converging-diverging nozzle, by exploiting the tendency of a jet to attach to a curved
surface, or by drawing on a counterflow. There is no vane in the stream, nothing to actuate and nothing
brittle to crack.

**Reading that against this article's own numbers makes the trade concrete.** The X-31 paid 103 pounds of
carbon-carbon in the exhaust plus 58 pounds of supporting structure, chose a brittle material specifically
to keep mass out of the tail, and accepted a jet deflection of sixteen degrees at forty degrees per second.
A fluidic system trades that hardware for bleed air, which is a thrust penalty rather than a mass penalty,
and its bandwidth is set by the injection valves rather than by moving a slab of carbon through a supersonic
stream.

**What has not changed is the quantity that governed the X-31's departure boundary.** A fluidic system still
produces a moment proportional to thrust, so its authority still falls as one over dynamic pressure and
still lapses with altitude. The mechanism is different and the scaling is identical.

**This is almost entirely a modern literature.** Of its 137 records, 124 were published from 2015 onward.

### Engine thrust with altitude

**Why the vectored moment falls with altitude.** Engine thrust and its variation with flight condition, in-flight thrust measurement and installed thrust.

**The control-authority argument in this article rests entirely on the way thrust falls with ambient pressure**,
and the working model of proportionality to the pressure ratio is a simplification that the
installed-performance literature exists to correct. Inlet recovery, bleed, power extraction and nozzle
matching all move the answer.

**The article reports the sensitivity rather than hiding it**, giving 0.7052 and 0.5922 at lapse exponents
of 0.8 and 1.2 against 0.6462 at unity, and the qualitative conclusion survives the whole range.

### The standard atmosphere

**The medium, named rather than assumed.** Standard atmosphere tables and their use as the reference for altitude, density and performance.

**Every altitude-dependent number in this article passes through a model of the atmosphere**, and the model is a standard rather than a measurement. Thrust lapse, true airspeed, dynamic pressure and Mach number all read from it, so an error there propagates into the control-authority argument and into the quasi-tailless dynamic pressure alike.

**The literature here uses the standard rather than revising it.** Beyond the tables themselves, these records apply it to density altitude as a performance standard, to landing distance, to flight reference simulation and to the reduction of altitude and airspeed in flight test.

### Axis transformations and the velocity-vector roll

**The kinematics of a velocity-vector roll.** Equations of motion, axis systems, quaternions and attitude representation.

**The relation that makes a wind-axis roll 94 percent yaw rate at seventy degrees is elementary kinematics**,
and it belongs to a body of work on aircraft equations of motion and axis systems that predates every
aircraft in this series. The X-31's contribution was to fly somewhere the distinction stops being academic.

### Flight control system design, actuation and allocation

**The system that made the aircraft flyable.** Flight control system design, fly-by-wire architecture, actuator saturation and rate limits, control allocation and incremental dynamic inversion.

**An aircraft with more effectors than axes has to decide how to use them**, and the X-31 had exactly that
problem with elevons, canards, rudder and three vectoring paddles. It solved it with hand-tuned mixing in
thirty-two software releases. The modern answer is control allocation as an optimisation solved at frame
rate, with constraints for position and rate limits of the kind this article computed for the vectoring
vanes.

**Incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion is the other major change.** The X-31's control laws were reactive
and scheduled on measured flight condition, which is precisely the architecture whose failure destroyed the
first aircraft. Incremental methods reduce the dependence on a model of the aircraft and therefore on the
accuracy of the air data that parameterises it.

Allocation is named in 59 of the 491 titles, and incremental methods in 30.

### Envelope protection and loss of control

**Carefree handling by another name.** Flight envelope protection, envelope estimation, loss of control in flight and upset recovery.

**Loss of control in flight remains the largest single category of fatal accident in several sectors**, and
the modern response is envelope estimation and protection computed in real time. The X-31 sits at an
interesting point in that history, since carefree handling is envelope protection by another name and the
aircraft demonstrated both its value and its cost.
**A pilot who cannot depart also cannot feel the approach to departure.**

### Unmanned combat aircraft and the tailless problem

**Where the quasi-tailless result went.** Tailless and flying-wing configurations, their directional control, and unmanned combat aircraft.

**The configuration question the quasi-tailless experiment opened is now the dominant one.** A combat aircraft designed for low observability wants no vertical surfaces, and an aircraft with no vertical surfaces has no directional stiffness and no rudder. Of the 289 records, 174 name a tailless or flying-wing configuration, and 20 name a yaw effector, a split aileron, a spoiler, a drag rudder or another innovative control effector, which is the direct continuation of the experiment.

### Clearing a learned controller for flight

**How a learned or autonomous controller is cleared to fly.** Run-time assurance, formal verification, explainability and certification of learning-enabled flight systems.

**The question the X-31 answered with six test pilots is now asked of learned policies, and nobody yet knows how to certify one.**

A control law of the X-31's kind is cleared by analysis, by simulation and by incremental flight test, and its behaviour between test points is bounded by the fact that it is a scheduled linear system with known margins. **A learned policy has no such structure**, and the assurance literature that has grown up around that problem is a distinct field, running from formal verification through run-time assurance architectures that wrap a learned or autonomous controller in a monitored envelope and revert to a conventional one when it leaves.

**The connection to this aircraft is closer than it looks.** The X-31 already carried the architectural idea in a primitive form. Its quasi-tailless experiment had a safety disengagement that reverted the aircraft automatically on a system failure or an envelope exceedance, which is a run-time assurance monitor in everything but name, built in 1994 because nobody was willing to fly a deliberately destabilised aeroplane without one.

**And the accident is the counter-example.** The one failure that destroyed an aircraft was not a control law behaving unexpectedly. It was a correct control law fed a wrong number, which is the failure mode that no amount of verifying the controller addresses.

**The whole of this cluster is contemporary and that is a fact rather than an omission.** Its earliest record was published in 2016, because the problem did not exist until a learned component was proposed for a flight-critical loop.

### Air data, icing and flush air data sensing

**The instrument that destroyed the first aircraft.** Air data systems, pitot and pitot-static probes, probe and airframe icing and its detection, and flush air data sensing.

**Flush air data sensing became a field**, and 47 of the 391 titles name it. The methods estimate free-stream conditions from a distributed array of surface pressure ports through a model, frequently a learned one, and they serve vehicles on which a probe cannot survive or is unwanted. Icing, of probes and of airframes, is named in 140 titles.

**The relevance to this article is direct.** A distributed array has no single pneumatic path whose blockage is shared by every downstream computer, which is the exact architectural property whose absence killed the first X-31.

### Airspeed systems as a measurement discipline

**Airspeed as a measurement.** Position error, pitot-static calibration, total pressure probes and the calibration of airspeed by tower and satellite methods.

**The instrument that destroyed the first aircraft has its own literature and it is separate from the flight-control one.**
Position error, static source calibration, probe placement and flow-angle sensitivity are the subject, and
the Kiel probe was chosen out of exactly that body of knowledge to solve exactly the problem it solved.

**What the discipline did not supply was a failure analysis for the case where the probe is correct and blocked**,
which is a different question from whether it is correctly calibrated, and every title in this survey that names the blockage of a pitot tube was published from 2015 onward.

### Analytical redundancy and sensor fault detection

**The cross-check, formalised.** Analytical redundancy, sensor and actuator fault detection and isolation, and fault-tolerant control.

**The cross-check this article performed by hand is now a standard technique with a literature.** Analytical
redundancy uses the known dynamics of the aircraft to predict what one sensor should read from what the
others read, and flags a disagreement. Applied to the accident flight it would have compared angle of attack
against airspeed through the lift curve and raised a fault when the two disagreed by eleven degrees.

**Nothing in that technique required computing power the X-31 did not have.** It required someone to have
written down the relation.

### Flight test, parameter identification and aerodynamic modelling

**How the aircraft gave up its derivatives.** Flight test technique, system and parameter identification, and the aerodynamic models that flight data correct.

**The X-31 corrected its simulator from flight through parameter identification**, and the same loop now
runs with far richer model structures. The modern literature treats the identification of nonlinear,
unsteady and hysteretic aerodynamics at high angle of attack as its own subject.

### Structures, materials and the airframe

**The airframe.** Aeroelasticity and buffet, the coupling of the structure with the flight control system, and high-temperature materials.

**The paddles were carbon-carbon because Inconel would have required nose ballast**, and the material was chosen knowing it was brittle. Carbon-carbon, ceramic matrix composites, high-temperature structure, exhaust-washed structure and thermal protection are named in 25 of the 88 titles. Aeroelasticity, flutter, divergence, buffet, gusts and the flexible aircraft are named in 43, and most of the rest join the structure to its control system or to its loads.

### Weapons, displays and the off-boresight problem

**The other half of the off-boresight argument.** Helmet-mounted and head-up displays, cueing systems, missiles and weapon system effectiveness.

**The programme's own recommendation was that post-stall technology needs a missile that can be launched off boresight at high angle of attack**,
and that combination arrived shortly afterwards and changed close combat more than the airframe technology
did. An aircraft that can point its seeker without pointing itself does not need to point itself.

**That is the strongest single argument against the X-31's own premise**, and the programme identified it.

Helmet-mounted displays and sights are named in 46 of these titles.

### The vehicle's own literature

**The programme's own record.** Every research record whose title names the X-31.

**This cluster is the one place where the contemporary survey has nothing to survey.** None of its 36 records was published from 2015 onward, and the latest is from 2012, which is what one should expect of an aircraft that stopped flying in 2003. Of them, 28 date from the 1985 to 1996 programme window. The modern work that touches the aircraft is computational, and it uses the X-31 as a validation case rather than studying the aeroplane.

### Other aerodynamic and flight mechanics literature

**The aerodynamic and flight mechanics residual, reported and not hidden.** Aerodynamics and flight mechanics of aircraft and flight vehicles that belong to no cluster above, among them manoeuvring flight, stability, performance, drag and wing aerodynamics.

**The period part of this cluster is the aerodynamics the programme was designed against**, and the modern part is what the same questions look like once computation replaced the tunnel as the primary tool. Of its 341 titles, 115 name a manoeuvre. **No further subject in it is large enough to name**, and dividing it further would describe the filing rather than the field.

### The general control literature

**The control residual, reported and not hidden.** Flight control of aircraft and flight vehicles, and the parts of control theory this article's argument uses, belonging to no more specific cluster above.

**This is the broadest cluster in the article.** An aircraft that is unstable in one axis, augmented in all of them, and dependent on a measured flight condition for its gains is a control-theory object before it is anything else, and the literature that surrounds it is correspondingly large. Of its 410 titles, 309 name an aircraft, a flight vehicle or flight, and the rest are the parts of general control theory that this article uses, being the control of unstable plants, robustness, gain scheduling, saturation, time delay and nonlinear control.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**Treating this aircraft through its keystone misleads in five places, and the first is the sharpest.**

### The Exchange Ratio Is Not a Property of the Aircraft

**The whole apparatus of this article treats the exchange ratio as a measurement, and it is better understood as a joint measurement of an aircraft, a pilot, a tactic, an adversary and a set of rules.**
The programme's own data proves it. The same aircraft in the same simulator with the same starting condition
returned 1.2 in one campaign and 0.47 in the next, and the programme attributed the difference to which
initial move the pilots chose.

**A number that moves by a factor of two and a half when the pilots change their minds is not a property of the airframe.**

### The Adversary Chooses the Engagement

**The F-15C and F-16C result is the boundary of the entire keystone.** An advantage that exists inside a
slow, close fight is realisable only if the opponent enters one. Against aircraft with enough excess thrust
to sit above the fight and re-enter at their chosen moment, the X-31's advantage was largely unavailable.

**This is an old lesson and the NASA history says so**, drawing the parallel with the [Fokker Dr I][ref_dr1]
of 1917, an aircraft capable of post-stall pointing that pilots of faster conventional fighters learned to
defeat by extending and attacking in slashing passes, denying it the ability to choose the time and place of
the fight.

### The Demonstrator Was Underpowered

**The X-31 fought the F/A-18 from a position of disadvantage in conventional performance**, and the NASA
history says so directly, attributing an exchange ratio of 0.37 without post-stall technology to the basic
mediocrity of an underpowered design against a more powerful opponent with a better dogfighting wing.

**That cuts both ways and the second direction is the more interesting.** An aircraft that loses almost
three fights in four conventionally and wins nearly two in one with post-stall technology has demonstrated a
large effect. But it has demonstrated it on an airframe whose conventional performance nobody would accept,
and the programme's own conclusion is that post-stall technology must be an integrated element of a design
rather than a bolt-on.

### The Angle of Attack Limit Is Not the Whole Capability

The article has treated the usable angle of attack as the figure of merit, because it is what sets the
aim-off angle. **The programme's own conclusions put velocity-vector roll rate alongside it**, and describe
the main advantages as apparent directional nose-pointing rate, which is actually yaw rate or
velocity-vector roll capability at high angle of attack, together with very high nose authority in pitch.

**Pointing where you cannot get to quickly is worth less than the static aim-off angle suggests**, and a
full treatment would need the rate as well as the angle. The rate is not published in a form this article
could use.

### The Simulation and Flight Numbers Are Not the Same Experiment

**The exchange ratios analysed at length in this article are simulation results**, from Pinball I and
Pinball II. The flight programme reported 407 engagements of which 325 were scored, and its conclusions are
stated qualitatively. **The temptation to read the simulator's 1.83 as a flight result should be resisted**,
and the widely quoted figures of thirty to one and of nearly ten to one over 103 dogfights come from yet
other accountings whose provenance this article has not been able to trace to a primary source.

**That inconsistency is itself the finding.** A programme whose keystone was a measured rate produced at
least four different headline rates that circulate independently, and the arithmetic above shows why that is
easy. The pooled value depends on the mix of starting conditions, and nobody quoting a single number says
which mix produced it.

**The condition under which pooling reverses a conclusion can be written down.** A set of per-condition
ratios supports a claim of advantage on average while the pooled figure denies it whenever

$$\frac{1}{N} \sum_i E_i > 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_i w_i E_i < 1$$

which is possible for any set that contains at least one ratio below parity, because the weights are free.
For the published set the two sides are 6.43 and 1.83, so both inequalities are satisfied with room to spare
in the first and by a margin of 0.83 in the second.
**The margin is what the knife-edge calculation above measures**, and it is smaller than the uncertainty in
the weights. The general form of that hazard is known in statistics as
[the reversal that can occur when groups are pooled][ref_simpson].

## The Source Base

**The research survey holds 6,685 research records drawn from the NASA Technical Reports Server, the Defense Technical Information Center through its registered identifiers, and the Crossref registry across journal and conference literature**, of which 669 are report primaries, being 10.0 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 2017.** Of the 6,681 dated records, 2,429 were published through 1999 and 3,922 from 2015 onward. **Every record the survey holds is cited**, in a cluster row of The Contemporary Literature.

| Period | Records | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Before 1985 | 745 | 11.2 percent |
| **1985 to 1996, the programme window** | **1,470** | **22.0 percent** |
| 1997 to 2014 | 544 | 8.1 percent |
| 2015 onward | 3,922 | 58.7 percent |
| of which 2022 onward | 1,789 | 26.8 percent |

### Where the Programme's Own Literature Lives

**The X-31 was reported almost entirely at meetings rather than in journals**, at the meetings of the
American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics and the Society of Experimental Test Pilots and at the 1994
High Alpha Conference. The tactical utility paper the keystone rests on and the close-in-combat results
assessment published a decade after the programme ended are both conference papers.
**The vehicle's own literature cluster holds 36 records, 28 of them from the 1985 to 1996 programme window and none published from 2015 onward**, and two of them appeared in a journal.

### The Equations That Carry No Citation, and Why

**Seven displayed relations in this article carry no nearby citation and that is deliberate.** They are the
weighting identity, the two ends of the two-point bracket derived from it, displayed separately, the tipping weight, the same bracket applied
to the other two comparisons, the flight-rate bookkeeping, and the ratio between the two simulation
campaigns.

**Every one of those is a construction original to this article rather than a result taken from a source.**
Attaching a citation to them would be false attribution, and leaving them bare is the correct treatment. The
underlying arithmetic is elementary and the reader can check it, which is the point of displaying it.

**The distinction matters because the rest of the article's equations are not like that.** The atmosphere,
the thrust lapse, the lift-curve slope, the drag polar, the turn relations, the binomial interval and the
divergence eigenvalue are all standard results with a literature behind them, and each carries it.

### On the Primary Record

**The primary record for this aircraft is unusually good in one respect and unusually poor in another.** The
flight reports, the quasi-tailless results, the yawing-moment asymmetry analysis and the tactical utility
paper are all public, detailed and quantitative. The NASA history published in 2014 carries a complete
per-flight log for both aircraft and the simulation exchange ratios by starting condition.

**What is not public is the underlying count of engagements and outcomes per condition**, which is the one
thing needed to attach an interval to any of the published ratios without assumption. This article works
around that by asking what various sample sizes would support rather than by guessing which one applied.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **17 of the 36 records in the vehicle's own literature are report primaries under that rule.** The rule does not reach the conference papers in which the X-31 was mostly reported, so 10.0 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

**The programme window is the row that matters for primacy**, because it holds the work published while this
aircraft was being designed, built and flown. A record from 1993 about high angle of attack aerodynamics is
a primary source for this article in a way that a review from 2021 is not, however good the review.

### Thin Subjects

**Ten subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group, and where it offers an alternative with the word or, either suffices.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the exchange ratio as a reported quantity | exchange ratio, kill ratio, loss exchange | 6 |
| agility metrics | agility metric, agility metrics | 17 |
| the velocity-vector roll | velocity-vector roll | 6 |
| turn performance and corner speed | corner speed, corner velocity, turn rate, turn radius, turning rate, turning radius, turn performance | 6 |
| the Herbst manoeuvre | Herbst, J-turn | 7 |
| control power | control power | 12 |
| thrust lapse with altitude | thrust lapse, or engine thrust, turbofan, turbojet, jet engine together with altitude | 4 |
| carefree handling | carefree | 10 |
| the icing or blockage of an air data probe | pitot, Kiel, air data, probe together with ice, icing, blockage, blocked | 21 |
| international collaboration in aircraft development | international collaboration, international cooperation, multinational, cooperative aircraft, cooperative development | 1 |

**The quantity the keystone rests on is almost never the subject of a title.** The exchange ratio, the kill ratio and the loss exchange together appear in six titles, so the aggregation and the intervals derived in this article rest on the statistics of proportions rather than on a literature of the measure itself.

**Agility metrics are a literature of the programme's own decade.** Of the 17 titles that name them, 14 date from 1985 to 1996 and one from 2015 onward, so the vocabulary the pointing argument needs was settled then, and the one modern title is a review of it.

**The velocity-vector roll is named in six titles, all from 1985 to 1996**, the decade in which the X-31 made it the command variable of lateral stick, so the kinematics above rest on the standard axis relations rather than on a modern literature.

**Turn performance is a standard relation rather than a measured literature here.** Turn rate, turn radius, turning performance and corner speed together appear in six titles, so the turn-radius comparison above rests on the relations it displays.

**The manoeuvre that carries Herbst's name has seven titles**, and the four published from 2015 onward are all control designs for flying it.

**Control power is thin as a title term and not as a subject.** Twelve titles name control power, six of them from the programme window, while the cluster on control power and effector sizing holds 60 records, because most of its titles name control authority, control margins or control derivatives instead. **The gap is in the vocabulary rather than in the work.**

**The thrust-lapse model that the departure and altitude arguments rest on is used rather than studied.** Thrust lapse, or engine thrust together with altitude, appears in four titles, none of which names thrust lapse, which is why the lapse exponent is carried explicitly above and the sensitivity to it reported.

**Carefree handling has ten titles**, three of them on helicopters, and one, a flight demonstration of tactile cueing, takes up the problem the X-31 pilots named, of restoring the cues that carefree handling removes.

**Pitot icing was described in 1938 and became a literature only after the accident.** Of the 21 titles that join a pitot, Kiel or air data probe to ice or blockage, the earliest is from 1938, the next from 2013, and 19 were published from 2015 onward.

**One title names international collaboration or a multinational or cooperative aircraft programme**, so the statement that the arrangement was itself a first rests on the programme's own record.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Control also names the control of power grids, gene therapy and bankruptcy law, structure also names crystal structure, vehicle stability also names the stability of cars, and manoeuvrability also names the manoeuvring of ships. Tailless also names cats, rats, batrachians and whipscorpions, and canard also names the foie gras duck. A delta wing is also a vortex generator in a heat exchanger and the cause of wind loads on a canopy roof, time of flight is also a measurement of particle detectors, cameras and cytometry, departure also names an airport lounge and a gate queue, binomial also names a waveguide transformer and an optical window, agility also names the agility of an organisation, upset also names a soft error in a memory cell, and carefree also names a way of life. Diesel combustion and exhaust, power transmission cables, radio-frequency calibration, buildings and bridges, and the timing of missile launches as a question of international relations are excluded on the same rule. Correction, withdrawal and retraction notices and addenda are excluded as well, because a notice of that kind is a part of the work it concerns rather than a research work of its own, and so are book reviews, conference reports, whole proceedings volumes, special-section introductions, numbered abstract-digest entries, figure and table records, software packages, teaching datasets, encyclopedia entries, news notes and meeting minutes. A second deposit of a document already counted, such as a report-series copy of a journal paper, is not admitted either, so that each work is counted once.

**The two residual clusters are held to a stricter rule.** The general control literature keeps the flight control of aircraft and flight vehicles, and general control theory only where it is the theory this article's argument uses, being the control of statically unstable plants, robustness, gain scheduling, saturation, nonlinear and high angle of attack control, thrust-vector control, handling qualities and pilot-vehicle interaction. It excludes control in other application domains, among them robots, ground and marine vehicles, power systems including the electrical power of aircraft, communications, process plants and traffic management, and pure theory tied to none of those uses. The other aerodynamic and flight mechanics literature keeps only the aerodynamics and flight mechanics of aircraft and flight vehicles, and excludes orbital manoeuvring, engine internals, aircraft subsystems, air traffic and target tracking. **The same exclusions are applied to every other cluster** for the kinds they name, being spacecraft and orbital manoeuvring, engine internals, the electrical power and electronics of aircraft, air traffic and airline operations, robots, marine and ground vehicles, multi-agent coordination, process and networked control, fluid mechanics and acoustics without a flight vehicle, and aircraft subsystems and ergonomics. Thrust-vector control of spacecraft is kept beside thrust vectoring, and ice protection beside air data and icing. **Every cluster is also held to the argument.** A record is kept when it bears on a subject this article's argument uses, and a method or phenomenon the argument relies on is kept when it is studied on another vehicle. A record whose only link is general aeronautics is excluded, among them structural health monitoring and the integrity, manufacture and repair of airframes, the design and sizing of transports, general aviation, electric and small unmanned aircraft, propellers, distributed and electric propulsion and engine internals, aircraft noise and the sonic boom, weapon bays and store separation, command and control and mission planning, orbit change, and civil operations. Aeroelasticity, buffet and high-temperature materials, inlet distortion and nozzles, and fighter and unmanned combat aircraft design are kept. A record whose only link is a shared word of control theory or a distant domain is excluded on the same rule, among them the stability theory of switched, positive, fractional-order and delayed systems with no flight plant, controllers shown only on laboratory rigs, the dynamics and control of structures that are not aircraft, simulator motion platforms, control loaders and other ground equipment, counter-drone tasks, infrared and radar signatures, radomes and the hydraulic and engine subsystems, and the reporting of atmospheric turbulence. The control of unstable plants with time delay or actuator saturation, motion cueing as it bears on handling qualities, and missile guidance against any target are kept.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Records from other fields that share a method with the analysis in this article are kept, among them Lanchester models of ground battles and other combat effectiveness models beside the measure of effectiveness, interval estimation and sample-size work from medicine and economics beside the binomial intervals. The otter board of a trawl, studied as a low aspect ratio wing at high angle of attack, is kept beside the lift-curve section. Aviation physiology and pitot measurement outside aircraft are kept on the same reasoning, and a reader may weigh each of them accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact, from the primary and official record.**

- Two aircraft were built by Rockwell International and Messerschmitt-Bolkow-Blohm and flew from
  October 1990 to June 1995, logging 580 flights with fourteen pilots.
- The programme was managed by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and flown by an
  International Test Organization at NASA Dryden, and was the first experimental aircraft
  programme administered by a United States agency as an international effort.
- Controlled flight at seventy degrees of angle of attack was achieved on 6 November 1992, and a
  minimum-radius one-hundred-and-eighty-degree post-stall turn on 29 April 1993.
- The first aircraft was lost on 19 January 1995 following ice accretion on an unheated Kiel
  probe, with the pilot ejecting and being injured on landing.
- The published simulation exchange ratios against the F/A-18 with post-stall technology are 0.36,
  8.5, 16 and 0.86 across four starting conditions, with an overall figure of 1.83.
- The tactical utility flight test flew 87 sorties of which 80 were scored, producing 407
  engagements of which 325 were scored.
- The quasi-tailless demonstration reached a time to double amplitude of 290 milliseconds at
  complete simulated tail removal at a supersonic condition.
- The second aircraft flew again from 2001 to 2003 in a separate programme with a flush air data
  system.

**Engineering analysis performed for this article.**

- The pooled exchange ratio is the mean of the per-condition ratios weighted by the losses of the
  denominator side. This is an identity, and it holds for every set of counts in which each
  condition records at least one loss on the denominator side.
- Between 81.9 and 93.6 percent of the aircraft's simulated losses must have occurred in the two
  starting conditions where it was behind. The bracket is derived analytically from two-point
  mixtures and confirmed by Monte Carlo over twenty-seven thousand feasible weight vectors, which
  ran from 0.8198 to 0.9356.
- At twelve scored outcomes per condition the defensive and high-speed line-abreast results do not
  separate from parity. The high-speed line-abreast ratio of 0.86 would need 691 scored outcomes
  to separate, against a few dozen flown.
- The loop gain on the accident flight stood between 2.890 and 12.543 times its design value,
  against a conventional gain margin factor of 1.995.
- The displayed airspeed and the vane angle of attack disagreed by 11.2 degrees at the moment the
  pilot remarked on them, corresponding to a dynamic-pressure error of 2.266, which already
  exceeded the design gain margin.
- Vectored control authority at thirty thousand feet is 0.6462 of its value at twenty thousand at
  the same calibrated airspeed, a loss of 35.4 percent.
- The post-stall regime offers no turn-radius advantage. Every radius computed at seventy degrees
  of angle of attack exceeds the 1,171 feet available at corner speed.
- The energy given up in a post-stall reversal from corner speed at 20,000 feet is 8,630 feet of
  specific energy and takes 46.0 seconds to recover, integrated.
- Against the steady asymmetry bound of 0.080, no arm shorter than the fuselage could hold the
  asymmetry above 237.6 knots calibrated at 20,000 feet or above 191.0 knots at 30,000 feet.

**Inference, where the record supports a conclusion without stating it.**

- The moment arm from the centre of gravity to the vane station is not determined. The departure
  on the second aircraft, at an asymmetry of 0.125 at 35,000 feet and Mach 0.4, bounds it below
  36.2 feet under the thrust-lapse model, which the fuselage length already guarantees, and the
  bound moves from 27.1 to 48.4 feet across lapse exponents of 0.8 to 1.2.
- The lift-curve slope of 2.769 per radian is inferred from a test pilot's recollection of a trim
  point rather than from published data, and is supported by falling between the unswept and
  swept low-aspect-ratio estimates.
- The altitude dependence of vectored authority is offered as the quantitative explanation of an
  effect the flight-test report describes qualitatively. The report does not make the connection.

**Claims the record does not settle.**

- **The number of engagements behind each published exchange ratio is not public**, so every
  interval in this article is conditional on an assumed sample size.
- **Two widely circulated figures could not be traced to a primary source.** They are
  approximately thirty to one, and nearly ten to one over 103 dogfights. Neither is among the
  simulation figures analysed here and the provenance of both is unresolved.
- **The effect of an airframe with adequate conventional performance is unknown.** The
  programme's own conclusion that post-stall technology must be integrated rather than added
  implies the exchange ratio would have differed.
- The yaw inertia is not published, so the directional stiffness of the simulated tailless
  configuration is determined only as a ratio.
- The velocity-vector roll rate achieved at seventy degrees of angle of attack is described
  qualitatively in the sources consulted and no usable figure was found, so the pointing analysis
  in this article treats the angle and not the rate.
- **The basis of the 2004 close-in-combat results assessment was not established.** Whether it
  reports flight or simulation figures, and under what accounting, is unresolved, because the
  full text of the paper has not been read.

## Out of Scope

- The detailed structural design of the wing and the German certification arrangements behind it.
- The Vectoring Extremely Short Takeoff and Landing programme of 2001 to 2003 in its own right,
  which is a distinct programme with distinct objectives and is treated here only where it bears
  on air data.
- The F/A-18 High Alpha Research Vehicle and the F-16 multi-axis thrust vectoring programme, both
  contemporaneous and both deserving separate treatment.
- Radar cross-section and low-observable design, which is the reason the tailless result matters
  and is not itself an X-31 subject.
- The design of the missiles the programme concluded were necessary.
- The organisational history of the International Test Organization beyond what bears on the
  flight-test method.

## Conclusion

**The X-31 was built to find out whether an aeroplane that can point its nose forty degrees further round than its opponent wins, and it found out that the answer depends on where the fight starts.**

That is a less satisfying result than the reputation, and it is a better one. The programme produced four
exchange ratios against a conventional adversary and the aircraft lost two of them. It produced an overall
figure of 1.83 which is a loss-weighted average dominated by the two it lost, and which sits three and a
half times below the average of the four.
**Between eighty-two and ninety-four percent of its simulated losses occurred in the conditions where post-stall manoeuvring did not help.**

It produced, in flight against front-line fighters, a clear advantage over the Navy types that would fight
it close and a clear disadvantage against the Air Force types that would not.

**An exchange ratio is not a property of an aeroplane. It is a property of an engagement**, and the
adversary has a say in which engagement occurs. The X-31 measured that with more care than anyone had
before, and the measurement is usually quoted as a single number by people who did not read the table it
came from.

**The programme also produced a result nobody was looking for that has outlasted the one it was built for.**
An aircraft with no vertical tail at all can be held at supersonic speed by vectoring, diverging at 290
milliseconds to double. That is now the central configuration problem of combat aircraft design and the X-31
answered it in 1994 as a side experiment made cheap by having already integrated vectoring into the control
laws.

**And it produced a lesson about instrumentation that cost an aeroplane.** A probe fitted to solve a real
problem at high angle of attack was not heated, its cockpit switch was not placarded, the hazard analysis
was not repeated, and the flight control system had no way to notice that both of its air data computers
were being fed the same wrong number. The information needed to catch it was displayed on the head-up
display, spoken aloud over the intercom, available on a standby instrument near the pilot's knee, and
computable in one line from the lift equation.
**None of those was a redundancy the design had asked for, and any one of them would have been enough.**
